title: The Quiet Hymn
premise: Zephyrine Zhou hosts a small-town overnight radio show, and for five years the dead have been calling in — voices of listeners who died days earlier, asking her to finish a hymn she's never heard. When sleep-recording software captures a second voice answering questions Zephyrine never asked aloud, she discovers the hymn is an inheritance passed through her family: whoever learns its last verse gains power over the boundary between living and dead, and every previous holder was consumed by it. Guided by a found family of listeners — a grieving widow, a teenage insomniac, and the ghost of her grandmother — Zephyrine must learn the final verse without singing along. In the end she refuses to claim the inheritance, teaching the verse instead to the chorus of the dead themselves, who sing it together and release one another; Zephyrine survives, keeps the show, and finally lets the calls go unanswered.
about_author: Noor Voss is the pen name of a former late-night radio producer who spent a decade on the graveyard shift and swears half the stories are true. They write horror about grief, small towns, and the things that answer when you talk into the dark.

chapters.title: Dead Air
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. During a routine broadcast, a caller named Marisol chats cheerfully about her week — then mentions her own funeral, held last Tuesday. Zephyrine plays it off as a prank, but after the show finds Marisol's obituary. The emotional beat is dread disguised as normalcy; the reader learns the rules of the show and Zephyrine's practiced denial.

chapters.title: The Second Voice
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. Reviewing her sleep recordings to check for teeth-grinding, she hears herself ask questions she doesn't remember asking — and something answering in a voice like hers but older. It names her great-grandmother. She brings the recordings to her only confidant, listener and audio engineer Dev. Beat: denial cracking into investigation.

chapters.title: Hymnal
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV, with a flashback to childhood visits to her grandmother Odile, who hummed a tune she forbade Zephyrine to finish. Searching the family church's records, Zephyrine finds a hymnal with the last verse torn out and a list of names — all Zhou women, all dead young. Beat: inheritance revealed as a curse.

chapters.title: The Widow and the Kid
chapters.summary: Alternating POV between Ruth, a widow whose husband calls the show nightly, and Priya, sixteen, an insomniac who has noticed the callers are always recently dead. The two listeners find each other online and compare notes. Beat: found family begins assembling around Zephyrine without her knowledge.

chapters.title: Verse One
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. The second voice — her great-grandmother Lifen — teaches her the hymn's first verse, promising answers in exchange. That night Zephyrine wakes standing in her kitchen, humming, having lost two hours. Dev hears the recording and begs her to stop. Beat: seduction of power; first real cost.

chapters.title: What the Callers Want
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV. Her husband's calls turn demanding: he wants Ruth to learn the verse so he can come back. Meanwhile Priya arrives at the station unannounced, having traced the pattern to the Zhou name. Zephyrine, exhausted and losing time, takes them in. Beat: the found family forms even as the dead grow hungry.

chapters.title: The Chorus
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. Every dead caller phones in during a single broadcast, singing in harmony, each voice a former inheritor. Lifen explains the bargain: the last verse grants dominion over death, but the singer becomes the hymn's instrument forever. Zephyrine realizes her lost hours were rehearsals she didn't consent to. Beat: horror peaks; stakes made explicit.

chapters.title: Odile's Tape
chapters.summary: Priya's POV. Digging through station archives, Priya finds a 1974 reel-to-reel of Zephyrine's grandmother Odile explaining how she refused the verse and paid for it with her mind. The tape reveals the escape clause: the verse must be given freely, never taken. Beat: hope discovered inside tragedy.

chapters.title: Last Verse
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. Lifen possesses the station's transmitter during the midnight hour, forcing the hymn through every speaker in town; Ruth and Priya hold the studio doors while the dead press in. Zephyrine sings the first verses willingly — then stops at the last, offering it instead to the chorus itself. Climax: refusal as victory.

chapters.title: Sign-Off
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV, weeks later. The chorus sang the final verse together and unraveled, releasing one another; the calls have stopped. On her last scheduled broadcast, Zephyrine thanks her listeners — living ones — and signs off the graveyard shift for good, keeping the family she found. Beat: quiet resolution, grief honored rather than undone.
